name: ThemeForge
overview: Automatically finds, scores and assigns theme songs for movies and TV shows.
description: ThemeForge searches YouTube with yt-dlp, ranks every candidate with an explainable scoring engine, and writes the winner beside your media exactly as it was delivered. High-confidence matches are assigned automatically; anything less certain waits in a review queue. Audio processing -- raising quiet themes, normalising, fades, trimming -- is available but off until you turn it on, so nothing is ever made quieter without asking. All decisions are recorded in a persistent index, so re-runs are idempotent and manual choices are never overwritten.

versions.changelog:
Build for Jellyfin 12.

ThemeForge now finds out who wrote the music, and the manual search does what an unattended run
does.

**Who wrote the music.** The composer's name is the most specific thing a search can ask for, and
Jellyfin records one for very few items. Without it the search ladder quietly drops its composer
phrasing, an upload that names the composer earns no bonus, and a title that is an ordinary word --
*Lost*, *Alien* -- has nothing to corroborate it and is held below the auto-assign score.

ThemeForge now looks the composer up in Wikidata and MusicBrainz, by the title's own IMDb or TMDB
id and never by name. Wikidata answers about three quarters of a library in a handful of requests;
MusicBrainz is asked only about the rest. Both are public-domain databases. Answers are kept for
two months, so a whole library costs a few requests once and nothing after that. Your library's own
credits always win -- this only fills in what is missing.

A new scheduled task, **Look up who wrote the music**, runs daily at 02:00 UTC, an hour before the
discovery run. **Diagnostics** now reports how many of your titles somebody is known for, which is
the number that says whether any of this helped on your library.

Lyricists, conductors and arrangers Jellyfin already knows about now count for half what the
composer is worth when scoring, and are never searched for.

**The manual search.** Searching for a theme by hand used to send a single query and never ask
ThemerrDB -- the weakest search in the plugin, on the page whose whole purpose is fixing a wrong
pick. It now asks the catalogues first, pins a ThemerrDB entry for the exact title at the top, and
runs every phrasing of the item's ladder, pooling the results before deciding what to look at
closely. A line above the results says what it did. Typing your own words still searches for
exactly those and nothing else.

It stays quick: the interactive search paces itself at 400 ms rather than the run's 1500 ms and
runs three phrasings at a time, so a seven-phrasing search takes about ten seconds.

**Fixed.** A search in which YouTube returned the same video twice faulted and showed an error
instead of results. Settings on the plugin page are now checked against the code that saves them,
so a control that would silently discard what you type fails the build instead of reaching you.

Build for Jellyfin 12.

You can now search for a theme yourself and pick a different one. Until now a theme that was
simply wrong was a dead end: the runners-up were only ever shown for items that had no theme at
all, so the only way to change one was to go and find a YouTube link by hand.

The control sits on the item page in Jellyfin, on every row of the Library tab, and on each item in
the review queue. It searches the moment it opens, with the same words an unattended run would have
used, and you can edit them and search again. Every result shows its title, channel and length, a
link to listen, and what ThemeForge makes of it with a one-line reason -- including the results the
rules reject, greyed out with the reason, because those are often the very video you were after.

A theme picked this way is recorded as your decision and no later run replaces it, whatever the
library's rule says.

The score recorded against an item is now cleared when you assign a different video, and that video
stops being listed as a runner-up that was passed over. Both used to be left describing the theme
that had been replaced.

Build for Jellyfin 12.

Themes are now written exactly as they were downloaded. Until now every theme was normalised to
-23 LUFS and faded in and out, and both were on by default, which made most themes quieter than
the upload they came from. Both are off. The best audio stream yt-dlp finds is kept as it is --
the same stream at the same volume, in the format it arrived in (theme.opus, theme.m4a or
theme.mp3) -- instead of being re-encoded to MP3. Nothing lowers the volume unless you ask for it.

Audio processing is opt-in under Settings: raise quiet themes to a floor (this never lowers
anything), normalise everything to one level, cut silence from the ends, fade, cap the length, or
always convert to MP3. A theme is only re-encoded when one of these has to change it.

Settings still at the old defaults are switched off for you; anything you had changed is kept.
"Re-download all themes", also under Settings, fetches every theme ThemeForge wrote again and
writes it with the current settings, without touching a single decision.

Builds for Jellyfin 10.11 and Jellyfin 12 are now published side by side, and the catalogue picks
the right one for your server.

the right one for your server.

ThemerrDB is now asked before anything that can defer an item. The retry backoff -- which exists to
stop a failing search from running nightly forever -- used to sit in front of the catalogue lookup
too, so every item that had failed once, or simply found nothing on YouTube, was invisible to
ThemerrDB for twelve hours to thirty days. Only a human decision or the library's overwrite rule
stops the catalogue now. "Nothing found" is also its own state rather than being reported as a
failure, and the retry button releases every backoff.

Everything the previous matcher gave up on is tried once more automatically.

The search finds more without accepting more. Season and episode numbers ("Season 1", "S01E01",
"Staffel 2") are qualifiers, not siblings -- the previous version rejected "Lost Season 1 Intro".
A year is evidence: the item's own year corroborates a match, and a different one ("Battlestar
Galactica (1978)" for the 2004 series) rejects it, brackets included. A subtitle of two or more
words stands for the whole title. Claims to be a theme are recognised in several more languages.

The composer Jellyfin already records is searched for and recognised, and soundtrack uploads on
rights-holders' "- Topic" channels -- titled by track, naming the show only on the album -- are
given a hearing instead of being discarded unseen.

Items with no theme now show what came closest and why, with a button to use one of them anyway.
The run summary says where its themes came from.

ThemerrDB is now asked first for films, shows and film collections, and its index is mirrored
locally by a daily scheduled task. Previously it was asked one item at a time and only about
films, so a scan spent one request per title discovering that most were not in the database. A
title that is not in it now costs nothing.

A series carrying only a TheTVDB id is matched by name against the catalogued shows, strictly
enough that "Girls" cannot match "Golden Girls". A film with no theme of its own inherits its
collection's, so Alien3 gets the Alien Collection theme.

Which catalogue answers first is stated rather than left to registration order: ThemerrDB, then
Plex's archive for the series ThemerrDB does not have.

A dry run no longer fills the review queue. It was recording the winning candidate and its score
before returning, so items the run would have assigned outright sat in the queue at full marks and
stayed after dry run was switched off. Those entries are cleared automatically.

Rebuilt how a theme is matched to a title.

The old matcher scored any candidate whose title merely contained the show's name as a perfect
match, so Lost matched "Getting lost in the woods ASMR" and Girls was assigned the theme for The
Golden Girls. Titles are now matched on identity: the name has to appear as whole words, a
one-word title has to match exactly, and any content word left over beside it -- "Golden" Girls,
"Lost in Space" -- means it names something else. Ordinary titles such as Friends or House go to
the review queue unless something in the candidate claims to be a theme.

Films are looked up in ThemerrDB by their TMDB id before any searching, and series can optionally
be looked up in Plex's theme archive by their TheTVDB id. A catalogue hit is the theme for that
exact title, so it is used as it stands.

Downloaded audio is measured before it is written, so a recap, a reaction or a stretch of dialogue
is rejected rather than assigned.

Per-library rules now actually reach the items they were set for, and saving one is verified
against the file on disk instead of assumed. A new Diagnostics tab shows the settings in force,
the rule resolved for each library, and why each item was passed over.

Settings lists no longer append to their defaults on every restart, so a keyword you delete stays
deleted.

Decisions recorded by the old matcher are marked as such, and "Start over" under Settings
discards them.

Fixes downloads failing with HTTP 403. The plugin now uses its own yt-dlp rather than an older copy found on PATH, and replaces it automatically when it ages out - previously the update task downloaded a current yt-dlp that was then never used. Adds a "Retry failed items" action to clear the retry backoff, a warning when yt-dlp is too old, and takes a settings snapshot per run so a mid-run change cannot make the report disagree with what happened.

Per-library rules for existing themes: leave them alone, replace only the ones ThemeForge chose, or replace everything. Adds a dedicated log file with its own level, full cleanup on uninstall, an action to remove every theme ThemeForge wrote, and a durable index that survives an interrupted run.

First release. Automatic discovery and scoring, loudness-normalised themes, per-library rules for existing themes, review queue, a persistent decision index, a dedicated log file, and full cleanup on uninstall.
